# My grooming van nearly caught fire. Looking tidy isn’t the same as being safe.

On Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was drying Moose in a client’s driveway in Bedford when I smelled hot plastic.

Moose is a Bernese. I had the dryer on high. At first, I thought the smell was coming from the dryer motor.

Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where the batteries are.

I shut off the battery switch and got Moose out through the side door, still damp. He was thrilled, honestly. Unexpected early exit from the dryer. Excellent afternoon, as far as Moose was concerned.

I also used the fire extinguisher a bit. I’m still not sure whether I needed to, but there was smoke coming out of the place where I keep two large batteries, and I wasn’t hanging around to see what happened next.

Everyone is fine. That is the most important part of this post.

But the positive cable connection was blackened, the cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres, and my van is now off the road for at least three weeks.

Moose’s mum brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook.

I keep coming back to that bit. One minute you’re doing a completely ordinary appointment. The next, someone is sitting beside you because you can’t quite stop shaking, and your whole income is parked in their driveway with a melted battery cable.

I’m writing this for the other groomers who read here, especially anyone buying a conversion or wondering whether their own electrical setup is safe.

And Tasha: please get the electrical details in writing before you pay that deposit.

## What was in my van

My conversion was built by Coastline Van Fitouts, by Darren, in spring 2025. The electrical setup included:

- A 3,000-watt inverter.
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt system.
- 4 AWG cable between the battery system and the inverter.
- A 300-amp ANL fuse.

I trusted it because it looked tidy.

The cables were tucked away. The connections were covered. Nothing about it looked like the sort of thing I should be worried about while I was washing someone’s dog.

I know now that a neat-looking installation does not tell you whether the cable is big enough, the connections were made properly, or the fuse can do the job it needs to do.

After the incident, Priya from Sackville Marine Electric inspected it. What follows is my understanding of what she showed me, with the technical findings attributed to her.

**I am not an electrician. Please do not use this post as instructions for rewiring your van. Get someone qualified to inspect your actual installation.**

I want us to know what questions to ask, not become battery-system experts between appointments.

## The bit about watts and amps that I wish I’d understood

The dryer uses roughly 1,800–2,000 watts. Sometimes there is also a water-heater load.

Those appliances get their power through the inverter, which turns the batteries’ DC electricity into AC electricity. The important thing I hadn’t appreciated is how much current that means on the **12-volt battery side**.

The basic calculation is:

**Watts ÷ volts = amps.**

So, ignoring losses for a moment:

- 1,800 watts ÷ 12 volts = 150 amps.
- 2,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = about 167 amps.
- 3,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = 250 amps.

But an inverter isn’t perfectly efficient. It needs more power from the batteries than it delivers to the appliances.

As an illustration, if it were 90% efficient at that load, a 1,800–2,000-watt dryer would draw roughly **167–185 amps at 12 volts**. A full 3,000-watt output would mean about **278 amps** from the batteries.

Those are examples, not measurements from my van that afternoon. Battery voltage changes, inverter efficiency varies, and other appliances add load. I don’t have a recorded current reading from when this happened, and I can’t say whether the heater was drawing power at that exact moment.

My first notes said “150–250 amps.” That gives an idea of the scale, but it isn’t a reliable operating range or an upper limit.

The point is that we are talking about a lot of current running through the battery cable and its connections.

Also, the “200Ah” on each battery is a capacity rating. It does **not** mean the battery can safely supply any current I ask for. The batteries’ discharge limits and their battery-management systems matter too.

Two batteries and a big inverter do not, by themselves, make a safe system.

## What Priya found

### The battery-to-inverter cable

The cable fitted was 4 AWG.

Priya told me that, for my 3,000-watt, 12-volt installation, it should have been 2/0 AWG.

If those labels mean nothing to you, they meant very little to me either. **2/0 is substantially thicker than 4 AWG.** It is not a small step up.

I’m deliberately saying “for my installation.” This is not a universal rule that every 3,000-watt inverter needs exactly the same cable.

The right size depends on the inverter manufacturer’s requirements, cable length, insulation rating, how the cable is routed, temperature, voltage drop and the current it must carry. The whole positive-and-negative circuit matters, not just the short bit you can see beside the inverter.

So please don’t take “buy 2/0” away from this post.

Take away: **ask a qualified electrician to confirm that your cable size is right for your inverter and the way it is installed.**

### The positive cable connection

The positive-end lug was another problem.

A lug is the metal terminal attached to the end of the cable. Priya showed me the crimp and said it had not been made properly. To my untrained eye, it looked as though someone had attacked it with pliers or a hammer rather than used the appropriate crimping tool.

I can’t tell you which tool was actually used. I wasn’t there when it was made.

What I can tell you is that the connection had been covered with heat-shrink, and I had never seen what was underneath.

This was where the damage was obvious: a blackened lug and melted insulation.

My understanding of Priya’s explanation is that a poor connection can add electrical resistance. When a lot of current passes through that resistance, it creates heat right at the connection.

You can therefore have a dangerously hot connection without the total current being high enough to blow the fuse.

That was a horrible little lightbulb moment for me. I had assumed that if something electrical became dangerous, the fuse would go first.

**A fuse is not a guarantee against an overheating connection.**

The cable size and the quality of the termination both needed attention. I’m not going to pretend I can separate out exactly how much each contributed to what happened.

### The fuse and where it was mounted

My fuse was a 300A ANL, mounted about 90 centimetres from the battery.

Priya said it should have been much closer, around 18 centimetres in the arrangement she was discussing with me.

Why does that distance matter? Because the section between the battery and the fuse is not protected by that fuse. If that section shorts against something, the fuse farther down the cable cannot protect the upstream fault.

I’m not presenting 18 centimetres as a blanket legal requirement for every grooming van. Applicable requirements and permitted arrangements vary. Your electrician needs to establish what applies to your system and how the cable is protected.

But “there’s a fuse somewhere” is not enough.

The fuse also needs to be properly matched to the cable and system. A 300A label does not mean it will protect any cable attached to it.

And there is another specification besides the amp rating: whether the fuse can safely interrupt the fault current the batteries could deliver in a short circuit.

The repair quote includes a Class T fuse. That is part of Priya’s proposed repair for my lithium system, not a suggestion that everyone should swap their fuse for one without checking anything else.

The fuse, holder, cable, batteries and inverter need to work together as a properly designed installation.

## What the photos showed me—and what they didn’t

Priya put my damage photos beside thermal-camera images of her own van running a similar kind of load.

The difference was wild. Mine had a blackened connection and melted insulation. In the images she showed me, her setup barely got warm.

That comparison helped me understand what she was explaining. It wasn’t a controlled experiment, and it doesn’t prove that every difference between our vans came down to one cable or one crimp.

But it made something very clear to me: this amount of heat damage is not something to accept as normal because a dryer uses a lot of power.

I have since bought a cheap infrared thermometer from Canadian Tire for about $40. I think having a way to spot an unexpected temperature change could be useful, **if your electrician shows you where and how to check safely**.

It is not an electrical safety certificate.

An infrared thermometer reads surface temperature. It cannot see through insulation or a bench seat, and shiny metal can give misleading readings. A reassuring number from one spot does not prove the connection underneath is sound.

Please don’t remove covers, reach near exposed terminals or run a suspect system just to get a temperature reading. And don’t wait for a particular number if you already smell hot plastic or see smoke.

## The smoke detector I didn’t have

There was no smoke detector in the back of my van.

There was only the one in the cab that came with it. I had treated that as “the van has a detector” without thinking properly about the separate work area.

I noticed this because I smelled it and then saw smoke. That is not the warning system I want to rely on.

As part of getting the van back into service, I want advice on suitable detection and placement for the grooming area, including the steam and moisture we deal with.

A detector would not have fixed the bad electrical installation. It is another layer of warning, not a substitute for safe wiring.

The same goes for the extinguisher.

I’m telling you what I did during my incident, not recommending that anyone stay inside a smoking van to fight a fire. Get yourself and the animals out, keep people clear and call 911 if there is smoke or fire. Only use an isolation switch if you can reach it safely. Don’t go back into danger for equipment.

## A power-off checklist for your own van

This is an **outside-looking-in check**, not a DIY electrical inspection.

Switch appliances off and follow your system’s shutdown instructions. Remember that switching off the inverter does not necessarily disconnect the batteries, solar, shore power or other charging sources. Battery terminals and some cables can remain live.

If you don’t know what is still energised, don’t touch it.

For this checklist, leave covers in place and use only what you can safely see without dismantling anything.

### □ Check for visible damage

Look at accessible cable insulation and equipment exteriors for melting, discolouration, cracking, chafing or scorch marks.

Look for cables rubbing on sharp edges or passing through holes without visible protection.

If something looks heat-damaged, leave the system out of service and get it inspected. Don’t run it again to see whether it happens twice.

### □ Take an unexplained burning smell seriously

Don’t assume it is just the dryer because that is the appliance making the most noise.

A persistent hot-plastic or burning smell needs investigating before the system goes back into use.

### □ Record the labels you can safely read

Photograph the inverter model, battery labels, visible cable markings and fuse labels without removing guards.

If you can’t see a specification safely, write down the question instead. You do not need to pull anything apart to earn the right to ask about it.

### □ Find out what each switch actually isolates

Do you know what your battery switch disconnects? What stays powered with it off? What changes when shore power is plugged in or solar is charging?

If the answers aren’t clear, ask for a labelled shutdown procedure.

### □ Look for storage problems

Are towels, bottles or tools crowding electrical equipment or blocking ventilation? Could loose metal objects fall into the battery area? Is there evidence of water reaching electrical equipment?

Don’t reach into an electrical compartment to tidy it. Have unsafe storage or access problems corrected with the system properly isolated.

### □ Check your warning and emergency equipment

Test smoke alarms according to their instructions. Check the extinguisher’s condition and service requirements, and make sure it is accessible.

Think about your exit route with a wet, frightened dog. Can you get out without going past the battery compartment?

### □ Gather the paperwork—or notice that it’s missing

Do you have a wiring diagram, equipment manuals, cable specifications, fuse details and any inspection or test records?

A missing folder doesn’t prove the work is bad. But it makes checking the installation harder, and I wish I had asked for more than a tidy handover.

**Please do not tug cables, tighten terminals, peel back heat-shrink or open fuse holders as part of this check.** Those are not harmless power-off jobs when batteries or other supplies may still be connected.

A visual check can find reasons to stop using the system. It cannot prove that the system is safe.

## Before you give a builder a deposit

Tasha, this is the bit I especially want you to keep.

Ask for the electrical specification **in writing**, before money changes hands:

- What inverter and batteries will be installed?
- What cable sizes and run lengths are planned?
- How were those sizes chosen?
- What fuse type, rating and interrupting capacity will be used?
- Where will the battery-side protection be mounted?
- How will cable runs be protected from rubbing and physical damage?
- What are the permitted simultaneous loads?
- What happens if the dryer and water heater run together?
- Who designs, installs and checks the electrical work?
- What standards or requirements are they working to?
- Will you receive a wiring diagram, test records and a shutdown procedure?

Ask about an independent inspection, too.

You do not need to understand every answer on the spot. You need answers that a qualified person can review.

“Don’t worry, we build these all the time” is not a cable specification.

I wish I had been more comfortable asking boring questions. I was excited about having my own van and getting to work. The electrical system felt like the builder’s department.

It was their department. But I was the person standing beside it with someone else’s dog when it started smoking.

## Why I’ve named the builder

I’ve thought about this.

I’m not trying to turn this into a public pile-on against Darren or Coastline Van Fitouts. I can only describe my van, what happened and what the electrician told me after inspecting it. I cannot speak for every vehicle they have built.

At the time of writing, Darren has not answered my three texts and an email. I don’t know why, and I’m not going to invent an explanation for him.

If he responds with information relevant to what happened, I’ll include that in an update.

But I also don’t think I should leave out who built mine when other groomers are making expensive decisions. Especially when someone I know is about to pay a deposit.

People can decide what to do with the facts. My strongest recommendation is the same regardless of the builder: get the specifications and have them independently checked.

## Where things stand

The repair quote is **$4,200**, covering rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse.

Parts are on order. The estimate is at least three weeks off the road.

I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far.

Insurance is still a “maybe,” not a yes. The adjuster is due Thursday, so I don’t yet know what will be covered.

I’m scared, honestly. I’m 28, I groom dogs around Halifax, and my whole income depends on that van being usable. Rent is due on the first whether I can work or not.

I’m grateful that Moose is fine. I’m grateful that I’m fine. I’m grateful to his mum for the coffee and for sitting with me when I needed someone there.

I’m also losing my mind a little over the appointments, the repair bill and the waiting. Being grateful nobody got hurt doesn’t make those things disappear.

If you take one thing from this, please let it be this: **tidy is not the same as right.**

Don’t panic and start dismantling your van. Get your paperwork together, ask the questions and have a qualified electrician look at the system you rely on every day.

I’ll post again when the van is back, with what was repaired and where things landed with insurance. For now, everyone is safe, the van is parked, and I’m waiting on parts.
